abstracts.010058: On the surface, English [Q+where] forms such as everywhere are locative. Yet as Sluckin & Kastner (forthcoming) document experimentally, they can also serve as impersonal human subjects, as in Everywhere in the UK loves Marmite, in which everywhere = everyone. The form retains its locative morphology and the pro-form where, yet it binds they/their and controls like a [+HUMAN] quantified indefinite pronoun. It must also be distinguished from ordinary locative (every place) and metonymic institutional readings. We argue that the impersonal use emerges from a distinct syntactic configuration in the nominal domain, rather than from lexical polysemy. Where spells out a higher locative D/P shell, while beneath it sits a silent, sortal, human-descriptive root √PERSON, selected by a relational categorising head nCAT bearing [uPlace]. Relationality comes from the categoriser, not from the root (cf. Adger 2013). The [uPlace] feature forces an overt locative PP into Spec,nPCAT, where it saturates the place argument of an inhabitant relation; nEA then abstracts over the human variable, and the quantifier binds the resulting property. Because the root receives its zero exponent locally under this categoriser, rather than from the higher shell, its human content remains active though unpronounced. Institutional everywhere, by contrast, retains a √PLACE structure with contextual transfer. The obligatory locative PP follows from [uPlace], whereas the macro-geographic restriction is an interface condition rather than a syntactic feature.
abstracts.010475: The placement of prosodic prominence in an answer is generally taken to depend on the question. E.g., "Who saw Mary? BEN saw Mary", but "Who did Ben see? Ben saw MARY". This correspondence is referred to as congruence, and in much of the literature it is captured in terms of grammatical machinery and constraints. I argue that such grammatical explanations are unnecessary in light of pragmatic considerations governing discourse, primarily those concerning the role of pragmatic questions, understood in terms of partitions. These considerations derive a more accurate empirical picture of question-answer felicity and do so in terms of general assumptions rather than specialized machinery.
abstracts.010476: Previous reconstructions of Middle Chinese posit Ming (明母) as [m], Wei (微母) as the labiodental nasal [ɱ], and Fu (敷母) as [pfʰ]. The latter two values, however, are hardly attested in modern Chinese dialects—a situation at odds with the general pattern that Chinese dialects preserve Middle Chinese features widely. Drawing on Dunhuang Sino-Tibetan transcriptions, the 'Phags-pa transcriptions in the Menggu Ziyun, historical foreign transcriptions, and modern dialectal databases, this paper proposes a new reconstruction: Ming as the prenasalized voiced bilabial stop [ᵐb]; Wei as the bilabial nasal [m], arising through the unconditioned change ᵐb > m and established as an independent initial through Song-dynasty standardization within the closed third-division slot; Fu as the voiceless glottal fricative [h]; and Feng (奉母) as the labiodental voiced fricative [v]. Re-examining the initial table prefaced to the Menggu Ziyun, the paper argues that Zhu Zongwen's double assignment of the letter ꡤ to Fei (非母) and Feng reflects the loss of the Qieyun Ming value in the Yuan phonological system and the resulting merger of Wei and Ming; the corrected assignments are ꡏ = Wei [m], ꡓ = Feng [v], ꡤ = Fu [hu], and ꡰ = Fei [f]. Dialectal evidence includes the acoustic agreement between [ᵐb] in Ming-initial words of Taiwan Southern Min and the Dunhuang transcription letter འབ (ɦb), the geographical distribution of [h] readings of labial words in Southeastern dialects corroborating the Menggu Ziyun transcriptions, and the zero-initial breathy-voiced rhymes of the Zhongyuan Yinyun ("房防", "墳焚棼", "扶夫蚨符芙鳬浮"), which furnish synchronic minimal pairs. On this basis we propose the Breathy-Voice Accommodation Hypothesis: the phonetic origin of the light labials is a zero-initial breathy-voiced closed rhyme formed when labial initials were lost from Bang and Pang words of the closed third division—words that in the dominant phonological system already belonged to the Bing class of clear-consonant-with-murmur syllables after medial loss. Subsequent developments depend on each dialect's capacity to accommodate breathy voice: accommodating systems retain the zero-initial breathy rhyme; non-accommodating systems substitute [v] or [hu], with [v] later devoicing to [f]. Wei [m] alone is the natural outcome of Ming [ᵐb], independent of this contact-driven evolution.
